head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Discovery time: when the DFS (Depth-First Search) first reaches u
Smallest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using tree edges plus at most one back edge
Detects whether the subtree has another route to u's ancestors
Don't go back along the edge we came from
Otherwise that edge would look like a cycle
Child's reach propagates to the parent
The child's subtree cannot reach u or above except through edge u–v
Then u–v is a bridge (critical connection)
Allows the subtree to reach an ancestor

p: 4 servers, cables `[[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[1,3]]` → [[1, 3]]. Events in order:

blocks.h: Why does `low[v] > disc[u]` mean a bridge?
p: `low[v]` is the earliest vertex (by discovery time) that v's subtree can reach without using the edge u–v. If even that is later than u, then nothing in v's subtree can get to u or to u's ancestors except through this edge; removing it disconnects the subtree. In the example the triangle 0–1–2 has a back edge so none of its cables is critical, while 3 can only be reached through 1.

bullets: Space: O(V + E) for the graph and recursion.

1192.takeaway: Tarjan's bridge algorithm: DFS with discovery and low-link times; an edge u–v is a bridge when low[v] > disc[u].

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: A lock plus the ability to wait for, and announce, a change
`with self.cv:` acquires the lock; `wait()` releases it while sleeping
The next number to print (shared by all four threads)
Only one thread's condition matches it at a time
This thread's rule (multiple of 3 only, 5 only, both, or neither)
Each thread acts only on its own numbers
`while`, not `if`: re-check after waking, since the state may have changed
Wake every waiting thread after `i` changes
Threads whose number is now due can proceed
Wake the others (so they can exit too) and return

p: Running the four threads for `n = 15` printed ['1', '2', 'fizz', '4', 'buzz', 'fizz', '7', '8', 'fizz', 'buzz', '11', 'fizz', '13', '14', 'fizzbuzz']; matches the expected sequence: True.

bullets: Exactly one of the four threads is responsible for each number, and they must run in order, so threads need to wait for their turn.
`wait()` releases the lock, so the thread whose turn it is can enter, print, increment `i` and `notify_all()`.
Busy-waiting (spinning on `i`) would waste CPU; the condition variable lets the others sleep.

blocks.h: A subtle point: the exit condition
p: When `i` passes `n`, threads still sleeping inside `wait()` would never wake without a final `notify_all()`. The thread that sees `i > n` notifies everyone and returns, so all four exit and the run ends.

bullets: Time: O(n) printing steps (each step wakes all four threads, so O(n) wake-ups in total times a constant 4).

1195.takeaway: Condition variable turn-taking: each thread waits until the shared counter matches its rule, acts, increments, and notifies all.

It cannot appear in all three arrays at later positions of the others, so it is discarded
Advance every pointer whose value equals the minimum
Handles ties for the minimum in one step

No more common values are possible

p: All arrays are strictly increasing. The smallest current value is smaller than at least one other pointer's value, and that other array will never show it again (its pointer only moves forward). So the smallest value cannot be a common element, and its pointer can safely move on.

1213.takeaway: Three pointers over sorted arrays: output when all equal; otherwise advance every pointer sitting at the minimum.

Equal ends wrap the inside palindrome
For `j = i+1` the inside is empty; `dp[i+1][j-1]` reads the untouched cell (0) below the diagonal

p: `'abcdeca'`, `k = 2`: the longest palindromic subsequence has length 5 (`acdca`), so deletions needed = 2 ≤ 2 → True. The upper triangle of `dp`:

blocks.h: Why does deleting the fewest characters relate to the longest palindromic subsequence?
p: Whatever you keep after deletions must be a palindrome subsequence of s. Keeping the longest one deletes the fewest characters: n − LPS. So the question 'at most k deletions?' is exactly `n − LPS ≤ k`.

1216.takeaway: Palindrome by deletions = n − (longest palindromic subsequence), computed with interval DP.

What it does

rows: Mark the cell as used, then undo it after exploring
Backtracking visited marker; the same cell may be used by other paths
Best continuation among the four neighbours
Cells with 0 (empty, off-grid or already used) return 0, ending the path
Gold here plus the best path onward
Try every cell as a start

p: `[[0,6,0],[5,8,7],[0,9,0]]` → 24. Best path value starting from each gold cell:

blocks.h: Why restore the cell after the recursion?
p: The visited mark must apply only to the current path. After exploring from a cell, putting its gold back lets other paths (from other starts or other branches) pass through it. Without the restore, the first exploration would erase gold for all later ones.

bullets: Time: O(m·n·3^g): from each start at most 3 new directions per step, over a path of g gold cells.

1219.takeaway: Backtracking DFS (Depth-First Search): mark the cell as used, explore four directions, restore it, and take the best total from every start.

When to reach for it

Every sequential-digit number is a slice of it
From low's length to high's length
Valid start positions for a slice of this length
A slice of length L starting at s needs s + L ≤ 9

Keep only the numbers in the interval

blocks.h: Why slicing and not counting up?
p: Only 45 sequential-digit numbers exist (9 of length 1, 8 of length 2, … 1 of length 9), so generating them all from the string is O(1) work. Looping through every integer from low to high could take up to 10⁹ iterations. The result is automatically sorted because shorter lengths are smaller and, for equal length, a later start gives a larger number.

1291.takeaway: Generate every sequential-digit number as a slice of '123456789' and filter by the range.

p: `'aababcaab'`, `maxLetters = 2`, `minSize = 3` → 2. Windows of length 3:

blocks.h: Why only the shortest length matters
p: A longer substring contains a minSize-long substring that occurs at least as often (every occurrence of the long one contains an occurrence of the short one) and has no more distinct letters. So the maximum frequency is always achieved at length `minSize`, and `maxSize` can be ignored. Counts: {'aab': 2, 'aba': 1, 'bab': 1, 'caa': 1}.

bullets: Time: O(n · minSize) to build and hash each window.
Space: O(n · minSize) for the counter.

1297.takeaway: Only the shortest allowed length can be most frequent, so count all minSize windows that meet the letter limit.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Value → all indexes holding that value
Lets us jump between equal values in one step
All neighbours of i: equal-valued indexes plus the two adjacent ones
Clear the list after using it once
The first visit to a value already queues all its indexes; scanning the same list again would make the algorithm O(n²)
Process one BFS layer per step count

p: When we first pop an index with value v, every index with value v is queued. Later pops of other indexes with value v would re-scan the whole list (all already seen). Emptying it makes each list scanned once, giving O(n) overall. With many duplicates (e.g. all equal values) this is the difference between linear and quadratic time.

1345.takeaway: BFS (Breadth-First Search) on indexes with edges to i±1 and to equal values; clear each value's list after its first use to stay linear.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: There it is the largest in its column and the smallest in its row (rows and columns are sorted in non-increasing order)
Everything below it in the column is also negative (columns are non-increasing)
Count the whole column part from row r to the bottom
Move left after a negative; down after a non-negative
Staircase walk: each step discards a row or a column

blocks.h: Why does this beat scanning every cell?
p: A negative at (r, c) means every cell below it in column c is negative too, so the part of the column from row r down is counted and the column is finished. A non-negative at (r, c) means every cell to its left in row r is also non-negative (rows are non-increasing), so row r has nothing more to count among columns up to c, and the row is finished. The pointer path has at most m + n steps.

1351.takeaway: Staircase search from the top-right corner of a doubly sorted matrix: a negative counts a whole column part, a non-negative discards the row.

`key=lambda c: ([-x for x in cnt[c]], c)`

Sorts the team letters (any vote string contains all teams)

p: votes `['ABC', 'ACB', 'ABC', 'ACB', 'ACB']` → `ACB`. Counts per rank (rank 1, 2, 3):

`sorted` is ascending, but a team with MORE first-place votes should come first. Negating each count turns 'larger is better' into 'smaller sorts first'. Since lists compare lexicographically, the first rank decides, ties go to the next rank, and so on; the trailing letter handles complete ties.

bullets: Time: O(n·m + m log m) for n teams and m votes.
Space: O(n²) for the count table.

1366.takeaway: Rank by a sort key of negated per-position vote counts, then the team letter.

What it does
When to reach for it

Top-down DFS (Depth-First Search): state flows to the children
Arrived from the right (this node is a right child)
Going left now continues the zigzag
Continue the zigzag or restart with length 1
Any node may start a new zigzag as a left or right step

p: Tree `[1,null,1,1,1,null,null,1,1,null,1]` (longest zigzag has 3 edges). Each row is a visited node (position = path of L/R from the root):

A child reached by a move that does not continue the zigzag still forms a one-edge path from its parent, so length restarts at 1 (the root has length 0 because no edge exists yet). Every node therefore starts a new candidate in each direction, so zigzags beginning in the middle of the tree are found too.

1372.takeaway: DFS passing the arrival direction: continue a zigzag by switching direction, otherwise restart at length 1.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Pending increment for each position, applied when the element is popped
Lazy propagation: record the add at the position `k−1` instead of touching k elements
Mark 'everything from the bottom up to i gets val'
On pop, pass the increment down to the element below
Elements below the popped one were also covered by that increment
Popped value plus its accumulated increment

p: `maxSize = 3`:

blocks.h: Why is it correct to push the increment down on pop?
p: `increment(k, val)` affects the bottom k elements. Storing it on the k-th element means: this element and every element below it get `val`. When the top element is popped it uses its own stored value and hands it to the element below (`inc[-1] += add`), so the elements below still receive it later. Pushing a new element starts with 0, because earlier increments did not apply to elements added afterwards.

bullets: Time: O(1) for push, pop and increment.

1381.takeaway: Lazy increments: store the add at the k-th position and push it down on each pop, making increment O(1).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Divisors come in pairs (d, x // d); one of each pair is ≤ √x
Add both members of the pair
A set avoids counting a square root twice (e.g. 4 = 2 × 2)
Add all four to the answer

blocks.h: Why a set and why stop at √x?
p: Looping to √x finds each pair once, so the cost per number is O(√x) instead of O(x). For a perfect square the pair (d, x // d) has equal members; the set stores it once, which is why 4 has three divisors (1, 2, 4), not four.

bullets: Space: O(1) (at most 5 divisors are ever stored).

1390.takeaway: Count divisors in pairs up to √x using a set, stop once more than four are found, and sum when exactly four.
